## Four kinds of evidence, arriving all at once

A recording hands you pitch, rhythm, and expression in the same instant, and the
obvious move is to type them in the same instant too. Try it on eight bars and
watch what happens. One duration comes out short in bar 2, every later entrance
slides half a beat forward, and by bar 6 you're hearing something that matches
nothing on the recording. You correct a pitch. Now you can't tell whether the
original fault was yours, the source's, or the fix you just made.

The trouble isn't that you made a mistake. It's that the mistake had nowhere to
be isolated. When one array carries four kinds of claim at once, every fault
looks like every other fault.

So give each kind of evidence its own turn. Pass 1 maps tempo, meter, pickup,
and phrase boundaries. Pass 2 enters attacks and durations on a single neutral
pitch. Pass 3 adds contour and a few anchor pitches you're confident about. Pass
4 settles the exact pitches, then articulation, dynamics, and the small timing
details. The representation gets richer at every stage while the timing
structure established in pass 2 stays put, available for comparison the whole
way through.

Hold that order even when a note seems obvious on first hearing. A confident
pitch will happily sit inside a bar that's half a beat short, and it'll sound
fine on its own. Keep uncertain events in the data and mark them with a
searchable comment such as `REVIEW`. That word turns a vague misgiving into a
queue you can work through: it says what still needs evidence without making
the rest of the transcription wait for it.

## One phrase, three renderings

The example plays the same four-beat phrase at three stages of the pipeline.
Integer notes stand in for MIDI pitches, because the relationship between an
anchor and an offset reads more clearly as arithmetic than as note names. Pass 1
shows up as the fixed tempo and the four-beat total wrapped around everything
else.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 76
use_synth :beep

rhythm = [0.5, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0.5, 1]
contour = [0, 1, 2, 4, 2, 0]
tonic = 60
exact_notes = [60, 62, 64, 67, 64, 60]

define :play_pass do |notes, durations, amp|
  notes.zip(durations).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.75, amp: amp
    sleep duration
  end
end

# Pass 2: one repeated pitch exposes rhythm without melodic distraction.
play_pass [tonic] * rhythm.length, rhythm, 0.6
sleep 1

# Pass 3: contour uses relative steps from a provisional anchor.
play_pass contour.map { |step| tonic + step }, rhythm, 0.8
sleep 1

# Pass 4: the exact spelling replaces the provisional contour.
play_pass exact_notes, rhythm, 1.0
```

Six attacks, four beats, three times over. The repeated C in the first rendering
strips out melody entirely, so all you have left to attend to is where the
attacks fall and how far apart they are. Count them. Then the contour version
climbs to a high point and comes back, and the final version replaces those
provisional offsets with settled MIDI numbers.

Here's the thing worth noticing. Every rendering uses the same `rhythm` array,
so the timing is bit-for-bit identical across all three. Does the second one
feel like the same rhythm to you? Most people find the contour version's fourth
note lands harder than the neutral version's did, and nothing in the durations
changed to cause that.

## Break one pass and watch it spread

1. Change the last rhythm value from `1` to `0.5`. All three renderings now
   finish half a beat early, because all three read the same duration array.
   Listen to how abruptly the phrase stops. No amount of pitch detail added
   later repairs a timing error inherited from an earlier pass.
2. Restore the rhythm, then change the fourth contour step from `4` to `3` and
   leave `exact_notes` alone. Only the middle rendering drops to a lower high
   point. That's a contour hypothesis being revised without touching the final
   pitch claim, which is precisely the separation the pipeline buys you.
3. Put `REVIEW` beside one entry in `exact_notes` and find it again with your
   editor's search. Write a short reason next to the marker, something like
   "upper neighbour obscures the attack", so your next replay starts with a
   specific listening question rather than a general unease.

## What each pass is allowed to claim

Each pass has a narrow contract, and the narrowness is the whole point. The
rhythm pass has to account for every beat in the meter, rests and ties included,
but it never has to name a pitch. The contour pass keeps that timing untouched
and describes direction only: same, higher, lower, and roughly how far. Exact
entry then tests candidate pitches against anchors you already trust, without
reopening a single duration. When two passes disagree, you know which one holds
the disagreement.

Pass 1 usually lives in comments or metadata, because its observations cover the
whole excerpt rather than any one event. Write the meter, your tempo estimate,
the pickup length, the source timestamps, and the phrase boundaries before you
enter a single note. Those phrase boundaries earn their keep as error
boundaries. Confirm four bars, reset your count, start the next phrase, and one
missing eighth note can no longer shift the remaining forty seconds of music.

The event schema holds still while the evidence changes underneath it. A
finished event carries `:note`, `:start`, and `:duration`, with `:amp` optional.
At the rhythmic stage, `:note` holds a neutral placeholder. At the contour
stage, it holds a provisional value relative to an anchor. Pass 4 replaces that
value with the settled pitch and nothing else about the structure moves. Stable
keys keep your diffs readable, and they let bar-duration checks run long before
the melody is fully known.

Programmers already have a name for this shape: it's a compiler pipeline. An
early stage establishes structure, later stages enrich the representation, and
diagnostics stay attached to the smallest unit that can carry them. The analogy
explains the discipline of the order, too. Skip an early structural pass and the
information you skipped doesn't disappear. It comes back later as a debugging
problem, in a form that's much harder to name.

## Why REVIEW beats a mental note

A marker in the data outlives your memory of why you left it. `REVIEW` with no
explanation is barely better than nothing; `REVIEW: beat 3.5, second attack may
be a tie` tells a future you exactly which three seconds to replay and what to
listen for. Grep for the marker and you have a work queue with locations
attached.

Resist the urge to guess a value so the marker can go away. An entered pitch you
don't believe is worse than an obvious gap, because it looks finished. Leave the
doubt visible and keep moving; unresolved events cost you nothing until you
claim the transcription is done.

## Eight bars, four saved versions

Take eight bars from one candidate in the source inventory you built in Lesson
42, and work them through a four-pass checklist built around one fixed event
schema. Save a separate version or commit after each pass, tagged
`p1-structure`, `p2-rhythm`, `p3-contour`, and `p4-exact`, so you can see what
evidence arrived and what stayed stable. Every bar duration must validate before
exact pitch entry begins, and every phrase boundary and anchor must be confirmed
before pass 4.

Aim for eight checklist rows, one per bar. Leave each unresolved event marked
`REVIEW` with a note naming the evidence that would settle it: a slower loop, a
clearer score page, a bass anchor, one more hearing of the attack. [Lesson 44](44-transcribe-by-ear.qmd)
takes the ear route through this pipeline, and [Lesson 45](45-transcribe-from-score.qmd) takes the score route.
The passes don't change; only the kind of evidence does.
